Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the solitary 3.1 cm recurrence in segment VIII abuts the middle hepatic vein and is technically resectable only if (a) the future liver remnant (FLR) after a segment VIII (or extended) resection remains adequate (≥30 % of total liver volume in a non‑cirrhotic liver, ≥40 % after prior chemotherapy) and (b) the venous outflow can be preserved or reconstructed. The structured analysis lacks the FLR ratio, detailed arterial/venous anatomy, and a complete thoraco‑abdominal staging; these missing pieces are decisive for confirming surgical feasibility.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Complete restaging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases that were not reported.  
- Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast plus CT‑based volumetry to calculate the FLR and delineate the exact relationship of the tumor to the middle hepatic vein, portal branches and biliary structures.  
- Review liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelet count, ICG clearance) to confirm that the remnant liver can tolerate resection.  
- If FLR is ≥30‑40 % and venous outflow can be preserved (or reconstructed), plan a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy/wedge resection of segment VIII with possible limited middle hepatic vein resection and primary repair or patch reconstruction.  
- If FLR is insufficient or venous reconstruction would be high‑risk, consider:  
   • Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology and possibly achieve tumor shrinkage; re‑image thereafter.  
   • Portal vein embolization of the right portal branches is not feasible because the left lobe has already been removed; therefore, alternative hypertrophy strategies (e.g., ALPPS) are generally unsuitable. A repeat limited resection after chemotherapy is the preferred approach.  
- After successful hepatic resection, administer adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (standard CRC regimen) and monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative FLR volume/ratio (critical to decide whether resection can be performed safely).  
- Detailed vascular anatomy of the middle hepatic vein and adjacent portal/hepatic arterial branches (needed to plan venous preservation or reconstruction).  
- Full thoraco‑abdominal staging (CT or PET‑CT) to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Information on prior systemic therapy and response (to gauge tumor biology and need for neoadjuvant treatment).  
- Baseline liver functional tests and ICG clearance (to confirm hepatic reserve).  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the lesion in segment VII is technically approachable and solitary, but a decisive piece of information – the future liver remnant (FLR) volume after a second hepatic resection (segment VII) – is missing. Without confirmed FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if prior chemotherapy has been given) the safety of an upfront hepatectomy cannot be guaranteed. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending FLR assessment (or a strategy to augment the FLR).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Step 2.1 – Confirm baseline data  
  • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate the FLR after a planned segment VII resection.  
  • Review liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, platelets) and assess for chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
  • Verify that the colorectal primary has already been resected; if not, schedule colonoscopy and plan primary‑site surgery (simultaneous only if low‑risk and no need for major hepatic resection).  

- Step 2.2 – If FLR is adequate (≥30 %/≥40 % with prior chemo)  
  • Proceed to curative‑intent surgery: anatomical segmentectomy of segment VII with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm negative margins (R0).  
  • Perform meticulous vascular control; preserve inflow/outflow to the remaining liver segments.  

- Step 2.3 – If FLR is insufficient  
  • Plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left liver (segments II‑IV) and achieve a safe FLR.  
  • Re‑assess FLR 4–6 weeks after PVE; if adequate, proceed with segment VII resection.  

- Step 2.4 – Systemic therapy  
  • Because the tumor is KRAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective; give neoadjuvant oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab for 2–3 cycles to (i) test disease stability and (ii) treat micrometastatic disease.  
  • Re‑stage with imaging after neoadjuvant therapy; if disease remains resectable, move to surgery.  
  • Post‑operative (adjuvant) chemotherapy with the same regimen for 6 months is recommended, provided postoperative recovery is uneventful.  

- Step 2.5 – Surveillance  
  • Serial CEA measurements (every 1–2 months) and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, to detect further recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and compatibility with surgery.  
- Confirmation that the colorectal primary tumor has already been resected (or need for resection).  
- Timing of the liver metastasis (synchronous vs metachronous) to gauge biological aggressiveness.  
- Baseline CEA level (useful for postoperative surveillance and to gauge tumor burden).  
- Details on vascular contact/invasion and hepatic arterial anatomy that could affect the technical feasibility of a segmentectomy.  
- History of prior systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, liver toxicity) which influences the required FLR threshold.  
- Date and outcome of the previous bisegmentectomy (complications, liver regeneration status).

MDT Discussion: Multifocal recurrence, assessment of resectability and local alternatives.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The MRI shows multiple 1‑2 cm metastases confined to segment III after a previous right hepatectomy, suggesting that a limited, parenchymal‑sparing resection might be feasible. However, decisive information is missing: (a) quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve after the planned segmental resection, and (b) a complete thoraco‑abdominal staging (CT chest/abdomen) to exclude extra‑hepatic disease. Without these data the surgeon cannot confirm that an R0 resection preserving ≥20‑30 % functional liver will be possible, therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending the prerequisite assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Complete staging  
   • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases (missing items in Extrahepatic section).  
   • Perform liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance (or similar) and calculate FLR volume using CT‑based volumetry; compare with the threshold of ≥20 % (normal liver) or ≥30 % if prior chemotherapy‑related injury is suspected (literature on FLR requirements).  

2. Assess primary colorectal tumor  
   • Verify whether the primary lesion has already been resected; if not, determine its location, stage, and symptomatology (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
   • If the primary remains in situ and is resectable, plan a coordinated “liver‑first” or simultaneous approach depending on patient fitness and tumor biology.  

3. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (if indicated)  
   • Because the patient is RAS wild‑type and CEA is markedly elevated (550 ng/mL), initiate a doublet regimen (e.g., FOLFOX) plus an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) to assess tumor biology and potentially downsize lesions, as supported by conversion‑therapy data in the literature.  
   • Re‑image after 2–3 months; evaluate RECIST response and CEA trend.  

4. Surgical plan (contingent on step 1 results)  
   • If FLR is adequate and no extra‑hepatic disease is found, perform a parenchymal‑sparing resection of segment III (or left‑lateral segmentectomy if multiple lesions involve II‑III) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion number and margins.  
   • Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage, aiming for R0 margins.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization of the right portal branches (already resected) or ALPPS‑type staged approach to hypertrophy the left remnant before definitive resection.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   • Pathology review for margin status; if R0 achieved, discuss adjuvant chemotherapy (continuation of the pre‑operative regimen) for 3–6 months.  
   • Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance every 3–6 months.

- History of systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, response).

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver lesions are limited in number (3) and size (2‑4 cm), but critical technical data are missing (hepatic segments involved, vascular/biliary contact, future liver remnant ratio, liver MRI). Moreover, the patient has synchronous bilateral pulmonary nodules (extra‑hepatic disease) and the primary colon tumour has not been resected or assessed for obstructive/bleeding symptoms. Current guidelines and the literature consider M1b disease (lung mets) an indication for systemic therapy first, and they require complete hepatic anatomical staging before a curative liver resection can be planned. Therefore resection is possible only after (a) systemic chemotherapy to assess disease biology and (b) completion of the missing imaging/functional assessments that are decisive for surgical feasibility.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy immediately (e.g., 5‑FU/oxaliplatin doublet + bevacizumab, or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) because KRAS is mutated and anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective. Aim for 4–6 cycles.  
• Perform baseline liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and a volumetric CT to define segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate FLR. If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) before hepatic resection.  
• Re‑stage after chemotherapy with repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT/MRI and consider FDG‑PET to confirm pulmonary nodule activity and exclude additional extra‑hepatic sites.  
• If hepatic disease is now deemed resectable and pulmonary nodules remain limited (≤4 cm, no mediastinal/hilar nodes), adopt a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   – Perform hepatic resection (major or staged according to FLR) while the primary colon tumour is still in situ, provided it is asymptomatic.  
   – Post‑operative recovery, then proceed to resect the primary colon tumour (segmental colectomy) once the patient is fit.  
• After recovery from both abdominal surgeries, reassess pulmonary lesions. If they are still resectable (bilateral but limited number, adequate pulmonary reserve), schedule staged thoracic metastasectomy (e.g., VATS wedge resections) after multidisciplinary thoracic review.  
• Throughout, continue adjuvant systemic therapy (additional cycles) as per response and tolerance, and maintain surveillance with serial CEA and imaging every 3–4 months.  

Step 3 - Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Detailed hepatic anatomy: which liver segments contain the three metastases, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and arterial anatomy.  
• Functional assessment of future liver remnant (FLR ratio) and need for portal vein embolisation.  
• Results of liver‑specific MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI) to confirm resectability.  
• Status of the primary colon tumour – whether it has already been resected, and whether any obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms are present.  
• Response to initial systemic chemotherapy (radiological shrinkage, CEA trend).  
• Full characterization of the pulmonary nodules (size, morphology, relationship to bronchi/vessels, FDG‑PET avidity) to determine resectability.  
These missing items directly influence whether a curative surgical plan can be safely executed.

The patient presents with three liver metastases (2–4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules in the setting of a left T4N2 colon cancer, without other reported sites. The presence of limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lungs) does not preclude a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be cleared. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically resectable. This situation is considered potentially resectable in a multimodal, sequential curative strategy, provided both hepatic and pulmonary disease are amenable to complete treatment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.
• Given the high CEA level (620 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given synchronous extrahepatic disease and high CEA (620 ng/mL), initiate systemic douhlet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab)
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The presence of nodular peritoneal metastases makes curative surgery unsafe at this time, but conversion to resectability is possible after systemic therapy that downsizes both liver and peritoneal disease. The MDT already concluded “not curable upfront,” indicating that a prerequisite (induction chemotherapy) must be completed before any surgical attempt.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months; obtain baseline molecular profile (RAS/BRAF, MSI) to select targeted agents.  
- Re‑stage after chemotherapy with high‑quality liver MRI (including hepatobiliary contrast) and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT; add FDG‑PET if not already performed to clarify extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Assess response of liver lesions (size, number, vascular contact) and peritoneal nodules (calculate Peritoneal Cancer Index, identify sites, evaluate hilar/hepatoduodenal ligament involvement).  
- If disease is stable or responding and peritoneal burden is limited (PCI ≤ 10, resectable nodules), plan a staged approach:  
   • Stage 1: control primary colon tumor – either simultaneous right hemicolectomy with liver resection if patient’s condition permits and adequate FLR is confirmed, or delayed primary resection after liver work‑up.  
   • Stage 2: hepatic resection – aim for parenchymal‑sparing, R0 resection of all four metastases; verify that at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage can be preserved. If FLR < 30 % (or <0.5 % body weight), consider portal vein embolization or ALPPS before definitive hepatectomy.  
   • Stage 3 (if peritoneal disease remains resectable): cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC, performed either concurrently with liver resection (if operative risk acceptable) or as a separate second‑stage procedure after liver surgery.  
- Continue peri‑operative chemotherapy: complete planned cycles (e.g., 6 cycles pre‑op, 6 cycles post‑op) unless contraindicated by postoperative recovery.  
- Enroll patient in MDT follow‑up with imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years, then 6 months, monitoring CEA trends (baseline 950 ng/mL is a high‑risk marker).  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Molecular phenotype of the tumor (RAS/BRAF/MSI) – determines choice of targeted agents and predicts response.  
- Exact hepatic segment distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and arterial anatomy – essential to plan a technically feasible, margin‑negative liver resection and to calculate FLR.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – dictates need for portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy.  
- Detailed peritoneal disease assessment (PCI, specific sites, involvement of hepatic ligaments) – decides whether peritoneal disease is resectable or will remain a contraindication.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction/perforation) – influences timing of colon resection relative to liver surgery.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) – impacts biological aggressiveness and urgency of systemic therapy.  
- FDG‑PET results and brain imaging – to rule out additional occult extra‑hepatic disease that could alter curative intent.

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- The primary rectal tumor is T3N1 and, according to current guidelines, requires neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (or total‑neoadjuvant therapy) before any definitive colorectal resection; therefore the primary is not yet resectable.  
- Five bilobar liver metastases are present. Resectability hinges on (a) the exact size and segmental distribution of each lesion, (b) the relationship to hepatic vessels/biliary structures, and (c) the future liver remnant (FLR) volume. All three items are marked “Missing” in the analysis, making a definitive technical assessment impossible at this stage.  
- A solitary right‑lung metastasis is documented, but its size, lobar location, proximity to bronchi/vessels, and pulmonary functional reserve are not reported (“Missing”). These data are decisive for pulmonary surgical planning.  
- Because key anatomic and functional parameters are absent, and because the rectal primary will need pre‑operative chemoradiation, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” It also does not meet criteria for “Not resectable” (no overt contraindication such as invasion of all major hepatic veins or unmanageable extra‑hepatic disease). Hence, it is “Potentially resectable” pending completion of specific prerequisite actions and acquisition of missing information.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Initial systemic therapy and rectal down‑staging  
   - Begin a conversion chemotherapy regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for the synchronous liver and lung disease.  
   - Simultaneously deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiotherapy for the mid‑rectal primary (TNT approach) to achieve maximal tumor regression before any surgical step.  
2. Restaging after 2–3 months  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define lesion size, segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   - Obtain a dedicated thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to characterize the pulmonary nodule (size, location, mediastinal/hilar nodes) and repeat pulmonary function tests.  
   - Re‑measure CEA to assess biologic response.  
3. Decision point based on restaging  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 % body‑weight) and all hepatic lesions are amenable to R0 resection → proceed with a liver‑first strategy.  
       a. If FLR is borderline, schedule portal‑vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (e.g., right hepatectomy after PVE, followed by left‑sided non‑anatomic resections).  
       b. Perform hepatic resection (major or combined major + non‑anatomic) aiming for negative margins, using intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm completeness.  
   - If hepatic disease remains unresectable after conversion → continue systemic therapy and consider ablative modalities (RFA/MWA, Y‑90 radioembolisation) or enrol in clinical trials.  
4. Management of the rectal primary  
   - After hepatic surgery and recovery (≈6–8 weeks), complete the planned total mesorectal excision (TME) – preferably low anterior resection with a diverting loop ileostomy, given the mid‑rectal location.  
   - Pathology will guide the need for adjuvant chemotherapy (continue/adjust regimen).  
5. Pulmonary metastasis  
   - If the lung nodule is ≤ 2 cm, peripheral, and pulmonary reserve is adequate, schedule a video‑assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection (or stereotactic body radiotherapy if surgery is contraindicated) after completion of colorectal and hepatic surgery, or concurrently if the hepatic procedure is limited and the patient’s physiologic status permits.  
   - If multiple or centrally located lesions are found, consider systemic therapy continuation and/or stereotactic radiotherapy.  
6. Follow‑up  
   - Serial CEA, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   - Consider enrollment in a surveillance protocol that includes liver MRI for early detection of intra‑hepatic recurrence.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Detailed hepatic lesion characteristics (maximum/minimum diameter, exact segments involved, vascular/biliary contact) – required to calculate FLR and plan resection strategy.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetry – decisive for determining whether a single‑stage hepatectomy, PVE, or two‑stage approach is needed.  
- Liver MRI results – essential for accurate lesion mapping and FLR assessment.  
- Status of systemic therapy already administered (if any) – influences timing of surgery and assessment of tumor biology.  
- Pulmonary nodule specifics (size, lobar distribution, relationship to bronchi/vessels) and pulmonary function tests – required to decide feasibility of lung metastasectomy.  
- Confirmation of whether the rectal primary has been resected or is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) – guides urgency of neoadjuvant chemoradiation versus immediate colorectal surgery.  
These missing pieces must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement associated with extra-hepatic lymph nodes, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has six hepatic metastases and radiologically documented hepatic‑pedicle lymph‑node involvement, both of which raise oncologic concerns. Critical information needed to decide whether an R0 resection is technically feasible is missing (future liver remnant volume, exact hepatic segments involved, size of each lesion, vascular/biliary invasion, and detailed nodal anatomy). Moreover, the disease burden (multiple lesions, KRAS‑mutated, very high CEA) makes neoadjuvant systemic therapy advisable before any surgical attempt. Because a specific prerequisite (down‑staging chemotherapy and complete staging work‑up) and decisive missing data (FLR, lesion size/distribution, nodal details) are identified, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate conversion systemic therapy: FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab, the standard regimen for KRAS‑mutated colorectal cancer, aiming for tumor shrinkage and assessment of disease biology.  
• Perform comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months (or after 6 cycles):  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  
   – High‑resolution thoraco‑abdominal CT or PET‑CT to confirm absence of additional extra‑hepatic disease and to characterize the hepatic‑pedicle nodes (size, morphology, metabolic activity).  
• Re‑evaluate resectability:  
   – If FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 %/kg) and all lesions can be cleared with negative margins while preserving inflow/outflow, proceed to surgery.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
   – If hepatic‑pedicle nodes are limited to the hepatoduodenal‑retropancreatic zone and respond to chemotherapy, include them in the surgical field; extensive celiac‑axis nodal disease would preclude curative intent.  
• Surgical sequence (tailored to intra‑operative findings and patient fitness):  
   1. Resection of the primary left‑colon tumor (either before, simultaneous with, or after liver surgery depending on symptomatology and operative risk).  
   2. Curative‑intent liver resection (major or extended hepatectomy) with en‑bloc removal of involved hepatic‑pedicle nodes, aiming for R0 margins.  
   3. If a staged approach is required, perform the first liver operation, allow hypertrophy (post‑PVE), then complete the second liver resection.  
• Post‑operative management: adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen as pre‑op) for at least 6 months, surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision)  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
• Detailed hepatic lesion characteristics: maximum diameter, segmental involvement, vascular or biliary invasion.  
• Precise anatomic description of the extra‑hepatic lymph‑node involvement (station, size, PET‑CT avidity).  
• Results of a liver‑specific MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI) and thoracic imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. still in situ, presence of obstruction/perforation).  
• Whether any systemic therapy has already been administered.  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

- Specific characteristics of the cerebellar lesion (size, edema, mass effect) and planned neurosurgical or radiosurgical treatment.

1. Initiate systemic therapy

   - If chemotherapy yields a good radiologic/CEA response and the peritoneal disease is limited (low PCI, resectable sites) and liver lesions become technically resectable with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 % / kg), proceed to a liver‑first strategy:

   - Persistent extensive peritoneal disease (high PCI, unresectable sites) or inadequate FLR despite down‑staging, continue systemic therapy with a view to palliative intent; surgery would be limited to symptom control (e.g., obstruction).

   - Adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for 3–6 months after any curative resection.

- Timing of metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and any prior systemic therapy or response.  
- Full thoraco‑abdominal staging: chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary disease, and a liver‑specific MRI.  
- Peritoneal disease quantification: total and regional peritoneal cancer index, morphology, and assessment of any ascites.  
- Results of a diagnostic laparoscopy (including PCI) and whether a PET scan has been performed.  

These missing elements directly determine whether the liver and peritoneal disease can be rendered resectable and therefore dictate the feasibility of the proposed multimodal surgical plan.

Woman, 66 years old, T3N1M1 transverse colon cancer, five liver metastases and two pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 420 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilateral hepato-pulmonary involvement, potentially treatable sequentially.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has bilateral hepatic disease (5 lesions) and confirmed pulmonary metastases (2 nodules). Current consensus and the literature excerpts state that definite extra‑hepatic disease (M1b) is an indication for initial systemic therapy rather than immediate surgery, and that resection of lung lesions should be planned only after the hepatic disease is controlled. Moreover, the structured analysis lacks several decisive technical parameters (future liver remnant ratio, hepatic segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, lesion sizes) and does not indicate whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been given. Because these missing pieces directly determine whether a curative‑intent hepatectomy can be performed safely, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of prerequisite steps (systemic therapy and complete imaging work‑up).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Initiate systemic chemotherapy now (e.g., 4–6 cycles of a doublet such as FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody, given RAS wild‑type).  
2. Restage after chemotherapy:  
   – Perform liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, segmental involvement, vascular contact, and to calculate the standardized future liver remnant (FLR).  
   – Obtain a PET‑CT (or at least a high‑resolution chest CT) to confirm the nature and exact size/location of the pulmonary nodules and to rule out additional extra‑hepatic sites.  
3. Multidisciplinary reassessment:  
   – If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % of body weight) and all hepatic lesions can be cleared with negative margins while preserving two contiguous segments, proceed to curative hepatic resection.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or an ALPPS/two‑stage approach before liver surgery.  
4. Surgical sequencing (liver‑first approach):  
   – Perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (or staged hepatectomy after hypertrophy) while the primary transverse colon tumor remains in situ if it is asymptomatic and resectable later; otherwise, resect the primary first if obstruction/bleeding risk is identified.  
   – After hepatic recovery (≈6–8 weeks), address the primary colon cancer with a standard colectomy (laparoscopic or open, according to tumor location and patient fitness).  
   – Finally, treat pulmonary metastases: if nodules are peripheral and limited, perform bilateral wedge resections (or video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery) after confirming adequate pulmonary reserve; if resection is not feasible, consider SBRT or thermal ablation.  
5. Continue postoperative/adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., additional cycles of the same regimen or switch to a different biologic) based on pathological response and molecular profile.  
6. Surveillance: CEA, CT chest/abdomen, and MRI every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then at longer intervals.

Step 3 – Missing data (most critical for decision‑making)  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or absolute volume.  
- Detailed hepatic anatomy: which segments are involved, maximum and minimum lesion diameters, presence of vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Results of liver MRI (or other high‑resolution liver imaging).  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and response to any prior chemotherapy (none reported).  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (already resected or not, presence of obstruction/bleeding).  
- PET‑CT or comprehensive thoracic imaging to characterize pulmonary nodules (size, relation to vessels/bronchi, mediastinal/hilar nodes).  
- Assessment of pulmonary functional reserve (spirometry) before planning lung surgery.  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T4N2 rectal tumor, six bilobar liver metastases, pulmonary micronodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1250 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MDT already judged the disease “not resectable upfront” because of six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules. However, resectability could be achieved after (a) systemic down‑staging chemotherapy (and/or targeted therapy) and (b) clarification of key missing technical data (future liver remnant volume, lesion size, vascular involvement, hepatic segment distribution, and detailed pulmonary nodule characteristics). These prerequisites are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, fulfilling the definition of “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT):  
  • Long‑course chemoradiation for the T4 rectal primary (45‑50 Gy with concurrent 5‑FU‑based chemotherapy).  
  • Systemic chemotherapy for metastatic disease: 6‑8 cycles of FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (RAS wild‑type) or FOLFOX + anti‑EGFR (cetuximab) to maximize tumor shrinkage and test disease biology.  
- Restaging after TNT:  
  • High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define lesion size, number, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
  • Chest CT and FDG‑PET/CT to characterize pulmonary nodules (size, number, metabolic activity) and to exclude additional extra‑hepatic disease.  
- If imaging shows adequate FLR (>30 % in normal liver or >0.5 % / kg body weight) and disease control (≤ 20 % progression, RECIST response), proceed with a liver‑first conversion strategy:  
  • Consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS if FLR is insufficient.  
  • Perform a two‑stage hepatectomy (or extended right/left hepatectomy with parenchymal‑sparing non‑anatomic resections) aiming for R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous segments.  
- Address pulmonary disease:  
  • If pulmonary nodules are limited (≤ 4, peripheral, amenable to wedge resection) and pulmonary reserve is adequate, schedule simultaneous lung metastasectomy during the second liver stage or a staged thoracic resection after hepatic surgery.  
  • If nodules are more extensive or patient fitness dictates, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or percutaneous ablation as alternative local control.  
- After hepatic (and pulmonary, if performed) clearance, complete rectal cancer treatment:  
  • If the primary tumor remains resectable after TNT, perform total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection) 6‑8 weeks after the last radiation dose, ensuring no residual liver disease.  
  • If the primary is still unresectable or symptomatic, consider a diverting stoma followed by reassessment.  
- Post‑operative management:  
  • Resume adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
  • Enroll in intensive surveillance (CEA, CT/MRI, colonoscopy) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
- Detailed liver lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameter, hepatic segments involved, vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Results of liver MRI (contrast‑enhanced, hepatobiliary) to confirm above.  
- Status of the rectal primary: whether it has been resected, symptom burden (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
- Pulmonary metastasis specifics: number of nodules, maximum size, lobar distribution, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and presence of mediastinal/hilar nodes.  
- FDG‑PET/CT findings to rule out additional extra‑hepatic disease and to gauge metabolic response.  
- Confirmation of whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
These items directly influence the feasibility of achieving an R0 resection with adequate liver reserve and safe simultaneous or staged lung surgery, and therefore must be obtained before proceeding.

MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of a single bone metastasis makes the disease oligometastatic but not curable without systemic control of the extra‑hepatic site. Curative hepatic resection therefore cannot be performed immediately; it requires (a) down‑staging of the liver lesions with systemic chemotherapy and (b) decisive information that is currently missing – namely the number, size and vascular/biliary involvement of the liver metastases and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. Until these data are obtained and a response is demonstrated, surgery cannot be planned.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy tailored to KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., oxaliplatin‑based doublet such as CAPOX or FOLFOX combined with bevacizumab).  
- Add bone‑directed therapy: palliative radiotherapy to the right iliac lesion (if symptomatic or at risk of fracture) and consider bisphosphonate or denosumab for skeletal protection.  
- Perform comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months of chemotherapy:  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT with liver protocol) to define number, maximal diameter, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR volume.  
   • Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   • Repeat bone imaging (CT/MRI) to assess response of the iliac lesion.  
- If imaging shows a sufficient FLR (≥30 % in a normal liver or ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑induced liver injury) and all liver lesions are resectable with negative margins, proceed to a liver‑first (reverse) approach:  
   • Major hepatectomy encompassing segments IV, V and VIII (extended right hepatectomy) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm resectability.  
   • If FLR is inadequate, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy before definitive resection.  
- After hepatic resection and recovery, address the primary colon tumor:  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic and no obstruction/perforation, schedule a delayed colectomy (segmental left‑colon resection) after hepatic recovery.  
   • If symptoms develop, consider simultaneous resection only when the hepatic procedure is limited (e.g., left lateral sectionectomy) and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits.  
- Continue adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen as pre‑operative) for at least 6 months post‑resection, adapting to response and tolerability.  
- If liver disease remains unresectable after chemotherapy, discuss alternative locoregional options (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion, Y‑90 radioembolisation, or percutaneous ablation) and maintain systemic therapy.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for final decision)  
- Exact number, maximal and minimal diameters of the liver metastases.  
- Presence or extent of vascular (portal/hepatic artery) or biliary involvement.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume or FLR‑to‑body‑weight ratio.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. intact, presence of obstruction, perforation or bleeding).

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T3N1 rectal tumor with two liver metastases and an isolated left pulmonary nodule at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 210 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, possibility of a combined approach depending on response.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has a limited hepatic burden (2 synchronous metastases) and a solitary left‑lung nodule, which in principle can be cleared surgically. However, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed until (a) the rectal primary is treated according to standard neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (T3N1 disease requires CRT/TNT before any definitive surgery) and (b) critical anatomic information is obtained – liver MRI to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and a PET/CT or tissue confirmation of the pulmonary nodule to verify metastatic nature and assess resectability. These prerequisite actions are explicitly missing, therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Induction systemic therapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild type) to assess disease biology, reduce microscopic disease and begin treatment of both hepatic and pulmonary sites.  
• Concurrent or sequential long‑course chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary (total neoadjuvant therapy – TNT) to achieve maximal tumor down‑staging and to permit a sphincter‑preserving low anterior resection.  
• Restaging after induction/TNT:  
    – Pelvic MRI for rectal response and circumferential margin assessment.  
    – Multiphasic liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT with liver protocol) to document size, segmental location, vascular contact, and to calculate FLR.  
    – Chest PET/CT (or CT‑guided biopsy) to confirm that the left pulmonary nodule is a metastasis and to evaluate its relationship to bronchi/vessels.  
    – Pulmonary function tests to ensure adequate postoperative respiratory reserve.  
• Decision point after restaging:  
    – If liver lesions remain resectable with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.5 % / kg) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to curative surgery.  
    – Surgical sequence (chosen according to lesion location and patient fitness):  
         Option A – Simultaneous approach: laparoscopic/mini‑open segmental liver resections (or wedge ablation if lesions are sub‑centimetric) combined with low anterior resection and a protective diverting stoma, followed by thoracoscopic wedge resection of the left lung nodule in the same operative session (if pulmonary resection is limited).  
         Option B – Staged approach: (1) liver resection first (preserving ≥2 contiguous segments, adequate inflow/outflow, biliary drainage); (2) after 4–6 weeks, low anterior resection of the rectum; (3) subsequently, thoracoscopic wedge resection of the lung metastasis (or stereotactic radiotherapy if patient declines thoracic surgery).  
    – In all scenarios, aim for R0 resection of every known site.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., additional 3–6 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to address micrometastatic disease, guided by postoperative pathology and CEA trend.  
• Ongoing surveillance with CEA, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or MRI every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for recommendation)  
• Liver lesion characteristics: maximum/minimum diameter, exact hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and arterial anatomy.  
• FLR calculation (volumetric assessment) to confirm that a safe hepatic resection is possible.  
• Confirmation that the left pulmonary nodule is a metastasis (PET/CT or biopsy) and its precise size and relationship to bronchi/vessels.  
• Status of the rectal primary (has it already been resected? any obstructive/bleeding symptoms?) and need for neoadjuvant CRT/TNT.  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered and the tumor’s radiologic response to it.  
• Pulmonary function test results to ensure safe lung resection.  
These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases and a single left pulmonary nodule in the setting of a T3N1 rectal tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not preclude a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.
• Pelvic MRI to integrate rectal treatment planning.
• Given the high CEA level (210 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation depending on response pattern.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the liver metastases.
B. Resectability assessment of the lung lesion by thoracic surgery.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged multimodal procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
H. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the current burden (8 bilobar liver metastases + moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis) precludes an R0 resection now, but resectability could be achieved after (a) systemic down‑staging chemotherapy and (b) acquisition of decisive missing information (PCI score, future liver remnant volume, vascular involvement). Both actions are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as first‑line treatment to achieve tumor shrinkage and to test tumor biology.  
- Within 2–3 cycles, obtain restaging imaging: contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT + liver MRI, thoracic CT, and consider FDG‑PET to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Perform diagnostic laparoscopy to directly assess peritoneal disease, record the total peritoneal cancer index (PCI) and evaluate involvement of the hepatoduodenal and hilar ligaments.  
- If imaging/laparoscopy shows a limited peritoneal burden (PCI ≤ 10) and a good radiologic response of liver lesions (≥30 % shrinkage, no new lesions), proceed to a staged curative approach:  
   • Stage 1 – Cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC for peritoneal disease (if PCI acceptable).  
   • Re‑evaluate liver disease after HIPEC; calculate FLR. If FLR < 30 % or major hepatectomy is required, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage clears the future remnant, second stage completes resection).  
   • Stage 2 – Curative liver resection aiming for R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
- Address the primary right‑sided colon tumor: if symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or at high risk of complications, perform right hemicolectomy either before systemic therapy (to prevent obstruction) or after liver‑first approach, depending on clinical urgency.  
- After completion of all resections, give adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX) and consider postoperative hepatic arterial infusion or targeted therapy based on molecular profile.  
- If response is inadequate, PCI is high, or FLR cannot be achieved, shift to a palliative intent: continue systemic therapy, consider liver‑directed therapies (radiofrequency ablation, hepatic arterial infusion) and/or best‑supportive care.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Total peritoneal cancer index (PCI) and detailed peritoneal involvement (ligament invasion, morphology).  
- Precise size, segmental distribution and vascular/biliary involvement of each liver metastasis.  
- Future liver remnant volume/ratio to confirm technical feasibility after planned resection.  
- Status of the primary tumor (resected or not, presence of obstruction/bleeding).  
- Molecular phenotype of the primary (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) to guide targeted agents.  
- Thoraco‑CT or PET‑CT results to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MDT notes that the liver disease is technically resectable, but several decisive pieces of information are missing that directly affect surgical feasibility. (a) The future liver remnant (FLR) volume has not been quantified (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing). (b) Comprehensive staging for extra‑hepatic disease (thoraco‑abdominal CT, PET) is absent (ThoracoCTScanPerformed = Missing; AbdomenCTScanPerformed = Missing). (c) The primary colorectal tumour has not been confirmed resected (Has the colorectal primary tumour been already resected? = Missing) and its timing relative to the liver lesions is unknown (Timing = Missing). Because these items are required to confirm that an R0 liver resection can be performed safely and that no contraindicating extra‑hepatic disease exists, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending those assessments and, given the unfavorable biologic profile (KRAS‑mutated, CEA 1150 ng/mL, 5 bilobar lesions with vascular contact), neoadjuvant systemic therapy is also indicated before definitive surgery.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Complete staging  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases (addresses all “Extrahepatic … Involvement” items).  
   – Perform liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % of total liver volume, plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage/ALPPS approach.  
   – Clarify whether the primary colon tumour has been resected; if not, schedule left‑sided colectomy (or simultaneous resection if patient fitness permits).  

• Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (biologic down‑staging and proof‑of‑time)  
   – Because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective; use a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab for 3–4 months (6 cycles).  
   – Monitor CEA and radiologic response after 2–3 cycles; aim for ≥ 20 % tumour shrinkage and CEA decline.  

• Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   – Repeat liver MRI with vascular phase to re‑evaluate the segment VIII lesion’s relationship to the middle hepatic vein and to confirm that all five lesions remain resectable with negative margins.  
   – Re‑calculate FLR; if still insufficient, proceed with PVE (wait 4–6 weeks) or plan a staged hepatectomy.  

• Surgical plan (once resectability confirmed)  
   – Perform R0 resection of all liver metastases: likely a right hepatectomy (segments V–VIII) plus non‑anatomic resections of segments II–III, preserving at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow; consider middle hepatic vein reconstruction only if necessary for safe outflow.  
   – Conduct left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) either before, after, or simultaneously with liver surgery depending on operative risk and patient performance status.  
   – Ensure intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any additional lesions and to guide margin assessment.  

• Post‑operative management  
   – Resume systemic therapy (completion of a total of 6 months peri‑operative chemotherapy) with the same regimen; continue bevacizumab for the full course unless contraindicated.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months thereafter.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for final decision)  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio  
• Thoraco‑abdominal imaging to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, nodes, bone, brain)  
• Status of the primary colon tumour (resected or not, presence of obstruction/bleeding)  
• Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous)  
• CA 19‑9 level (another prognostic marker)  
• Arterial and biliary anatomy of the involved segments (to plan vascular control and biliary drainage)  
• Any prior systemic therapy already given and its response  
• Patient performance status and comorbidities (to confirm fitness for major hepatectomy).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is potentially resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Precise segmental distribution of the three lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. a chest CT scan
E. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has extensive hepatic disease (seven lesions up to 5 cm) with no documented assessment of hepatic segment distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, or future liver remnant (FLR) volume. These missing technical parameters prevent confirmation of a margin‑negative resection while preserving adequate liver function. Moreover, the aggressive biology (BRAF V600E, CEA 1600 ng/mL) warrants neoadjuvant systemic therapy to test tumor chemosensitivity (“proof of time”) before committing to surgery. Thus a prerequisite (systemic down‑staging and complete imaging/FLR assessment) must be fulfilled prior to any operative plan, fitting the definition of “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive first‑line systemic therapy appropriate for BRAF‑mutated mCRC (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or the BEACON regimen: encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib).  
- After 2–3 months, obtain high‑quality liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define segmental involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and to calculate FLR volume.  
- Re‑stage disease: if all liver lesions are still present but have responded (≥30 % shrinkage) and FLR is ≥30 % (or ≥20 % in a non‑steatotic liver), proceed to curative‑intent hepatic surgery.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, then reassess.  
   • Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy if lesions are bilobar and cannot be cleared in a single operation.  
- Primary colorectal tumor: if still unresected, schedule resection after hepatic clearance (liver‑first strategy) or simultaneous resection if the primary is asymptomatic, technically feasible, and the patient’s performance status permits.  
- Post‑operative: give adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance) for at least 6 months, with close CEA monitoring and imaging every 3 months for the first year.  
- If disease progresses on neoadjuvant therapy or FLR cannot be achieved, shift to a palliative approach (systemic therapy ± liver‑directed locoregional treatments such as Y‑90 radioembolization or thermal ablation).

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed hepatic anatomy: segments involved, vascular and biliary contact, and presence of necrosis/fibrosis.  
- Quantitative FLR ratio (or volumetric assessment).  
- Liver MRI results to confirm lesion distribution and resectability.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) to refine biological risk.  
- Status of the primary tumor (resected or not) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms.  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and baseline liver function (to gauge surgical fitness).  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 7 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

• The elevated CEA level (1600 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.

• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in the rare situation of major radiologic and biologic response with marked reduction in number and size of lesions. 
• In this situation, first multiple atypical resections and ablation guided by ultrasound with the aim to obtain R0 margins.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective.

• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, T3N2 upper rectal cancer with four liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 980 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases with MSI-H profile opening discussion for first-line immunotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – resection cannot be planned at this time because decisive information is missing. Specifically, a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (to define lesion size, segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement) and an accurate future liver remnant (FLR) volumetric assessment are required before a technical feasibility judgment can be made. Until these data are obtained, surgery must be deferred and a systemic‑first approach is indicated.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Baseline imaging: obtain a liver‑specific MRI and a high‑resolution pelvic MRI; perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR.  
- Systemic therapy: initiate first‑line PD‑1‑directed immunotherapy (e.g., pembrolizumab 200 mg q3 weeks) given the MSI‑H, RAS‑wild‑type metastatic profile. This aligns with phase‑III data showing superior PFS and response rates in MSI‑H mCRC.  
- Restaging: repeat MRI of liver and pelvis after 8–12 weeks of immunotherapy to assess tumor response, FLR adequacy, and any new extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Decision point after restaging:  
  • If liver disease shows partial/complete response and imaging confirms that all metastases can be resected with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % in a cirrhotic liver) and negative margins are achievable, proceed with a liver‑first surgical plan.  
  • Plan a staged hepatectomy if bilateral disease requires major resection; consider portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR is borderline.  
  • After hepatic clearance, address the primary rectal tumor. If the primary remains T3N2 but is asymptomatic, schedule long‑course chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) 6–8 weeks later (standard TNT sequence). If the primary becomes symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding), insert a diverting stoma or give short‑course RT as bridge.  
- Adjuvant therapy: complete the immunotherapy course (minimum 6 months) and consider additional adjuvant chemotherapy per multidisciplinary consensus, especially given the high nodal stage (N2).  
- Surveillance: CEA and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.

Man, 55 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, nine bilobar metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2500 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.Liver  MRI: infiltration of the right portal pedicle.
MDT Discussion: Major liver involvement, vascular invasion compromising resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
The liver assessment shows nine bilobar metastases with true vascular invasion (right portal pedicle infiltration) and no clear FLR estimate. According to the structured analysis, “PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion: True” and “FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing.” The MDT comment that vascular invasion “compromises resectability” indicates that an immediate R0 resection is not feasible. However, conversion chemotherapy and/or portal vein embolization can downsize disease and improve FLR, making resection possible. Therefore the case meets the definition of “Potentially resectable” because a specific prerequisite action – conversion systemic therapy (and possibly PVE) – must be completed before surgery.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate conversion systemic therapy tailored to KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., oxaliplatin‑based doublet such as mFOLFOX6 plus bevacizumab).  
- Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) after 2–3 cycles (≈6 weeks) to assess tumor response, especially reduction of portal pedicle involvement and overall tumor burden.  
- If response is adequate but FLR is still <30 % of total liver volume, schedule portal vein embolization of the right portal branch to induce hypertrophy of the left liver.  
- Re‑evaluate FLR 2–3 weeks after PVE; when FLR ≥30 % and vascular invasion has regressed sufficiently, plan a staged hepatic resection:  
   • First stage – right hepatectomy (or extended right hepatectomy) with vascular reconstruction as needed, aiming for R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous left‑liver segments.  
   • Second stage – after recovery and confirmation of adequate liver function, perform left‑lobe parenchymal‑sparing resections or ablations of remaining lesions to achieve complete clearance.  
- Adopt a liver‑first sequence because the primary tumor is asymptomatic (no obstruction, perforation, or bleeding). Perform right hemicolectomy after hepatic surgery once the patient has recovered, provided oncologic timing allows.  
- Continue postoperative systemic therapy (e.g., additional cycles of FOLFOX‑bevacizumab or switch to FOLFIRI if progression) for 6 months as adjuvant treatment, monitoring CEA and imaging.  
- Throughout, maintain multidisciplinary review (medical oncology, hepatobiliary surgery, radiology) to adjust plan based on response and liver function.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric assessment – essential to decide on PVE or staged resection.  
- Exact size and segmental distribution of each metastasis – needed for surgical planning and to calculate tumor burden.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. not resected) – determines timing of colon resection.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered – influences choice of regimen and timing of surgery.  
- Detailed arterial and portal venous anatomy, including extent of portal pedicle infiltration – critical for planning vascular reconstruction or determining feasibility of resection.  
These missing items are the most decisive for finalizing resectability and tailoring the operative approach.

- Status of systemic therapy already given (has any chemotherapy been started?).  
- Complete extra‑hepatic staging (CT chest/abdomen) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal or bone metastases.

- Patient’s performance status and comorbidities (to assess fitness for combined or staged major surgery).

Response:

Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver MRI shows a segment VII metastasis with >1 cm IVC invasion, a technical factor that usually precludes upfront R0 resection without vascular reconstruction. Moreover, key information required to judge feasibility is missing – no thoraco‑abdominal CT to rule out extra‑hepatic disease, no calculation of future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and no record of prior systemic therapy that could downsize the lesion and test tumor biology. Because a specific prerequisite (pre‑operative systemic chemotherapy and further imaging/FLR assessment) is needed before a safe hepatic resection can be planned, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy immediately (e.g., 4‑6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑VEGF; RAS‑wild type also allows addition of anti‑EGFR if deemed appropriate) to (a) assess disease biology, (b) attempt down‑staging of the IVC‑invasive lesion, and (c) treat occult micrometastatic disease.

   – If the IVC invasion regresses to limited contact (< 180°) or becomes resectable with clear margins, schedule a liver‑first approach: (1) hepatic resection with en‑bloc IVC segment resection and reconstruction (using prosthetic graft or autologous conduit) while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments; (2) subsequently address the primary left‑colon tumor (either simultaneous if operative risk acceptable, or delayed after hepatic recovery).

• Status of the colorectal primary (has it been resected or not).  
• Complete thoraco‑abdominal imaging to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
• Details of arterial and portal venous anatomy around the segment VII lesion.  
• Extent and exact pattern of IVC invasion (length of wall involvement, circumferential encasement).  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered and the tumor’s radiologic response.  
These missing items directly determine whether a curative‑intent hepatic resection with vascular reconstruction is feasible or whether the patient should remain on systemic therapy alone.

• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical strategy if feasibility is confirmed
• If significant regression occurs, plan a complex parenchymal-sparing resection guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Anticipate possible portal vein control or reconstruction depending on residual contact.
• Address additional lesions with wedge/segmental resections.

E. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

A. Precise relationship of the segment IVb lesion to right and left portal branches on MRI.
B. Exact segmental distribution of the other four lesions.
C. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of two-stage strategy with major hepatectomy.
D. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA

H. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy

Case_Content:
Man, 73 years old, transverse colon tumor, two liver metastases (4.2 and 4.8 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 70 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Normal CEA despite high volume, question regarding biological sensitivity for follow-up.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the case lacks several decisive pieces of information that are required to confirm that a margin‑negative (R0) liver resection can be performed safely. Specifically, the hepatic segments involved, any vascular or biliary contact, and the calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio are missing. In addition, a liver‑specific MRI, which is recommended for accurate anatomic mapping, has not been performed. Because these items are essential for determining whether the two lesions (4.2 cm and 4.8 cm) can be removed while preserving ≥30 % functional liver (or ≥20 % in patients pre‑treated with chemotherapy), the disease cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- 1. Complete staging work‑up  
  • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (preferably with hepatobiliary agent) to define lesion location, relationship to portal/hepatic veins and biliary structures, and to calculate the FLR.  
  • Clarify whether the primary transverse colon tumor has already been resected; if not, plan either simultaneous colon‑liver resection (if patient fitness allows) or staged resection (colon first, then liver).  
  • Determine timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) to guide sequencing.  

- 2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (biologic “proof of time”)  
  • Because the tumour is RAS‑wild‑type and BRAF‑wild‑type, initiate a doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab).  
  • Treat for 2–3 months (≈4–6 cycles) and reassess radiologically (CT/MRI) for response and for any progression of disease.  

- 3. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
  • If imaging shows that both lesions remain resectable with adequate FLR, proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
  • If lesions are close to major vessels or FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to augment remnant volume before definitive resection.  

- 4. Surgical plan  
  • Aim for R0 resection of all liver metastases, preserving at least two contiguous hepatic segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
  • Perform primary colon resection with oncologic margins (≥1 mm) either simultaneously or in a staged fashion, based on patient’s performance status and operative risk.  

- 5. Post‑operative management  
  • Resume/adapt systemic therapy post‑operatively (e.g., 6 months of the same regimen) as adjuvant treatment, unless contraindicated.  
  • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then at increasing intervals.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
- Hepatic segment(s) involved and relationship of each metastasis to portal/hepatic vessels and biliary ducts.  
- Calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio (or volumetric assessment).  
- Results of a liver‑specific MRI (or equivalent high‑resolution imaging).  
- Status of the primary transverse colon tumour (resected vs unresected).  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) to decide on simultaneous versus staged resection.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  

These missing items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
